title: The Ceasefire Was Twelve Days Old. Then Two More Ships Were Hit and Trump Threatened to Erase Iran.
excerpt: A second tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz triggered fresh US strikes on Saturday — the worst escalation since the peace deal was signed. Oil markets are closed. India, which just started breathing easier, is holding its breath again.
body:
Twelve days. That is how long the ceasefire between the United States and Iran lasted before both sides were once again exchanging missile strikes over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passage through which a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas travels.

On Saturday, a Panama-flagged tanker was struck by an Iranian drone in the strait, the second commercial vessel hit in three days. The United States responded within hours, launching what US Central Command called strikes against Iranian military surveillance, communications, air defence, drone storage and mine-laying facilities around the waterway. Explosions were reported in the Iranian port of Sirik early Sunday morning local time.

"Iran was given a chance to honour the ceasefire agreement but elected not to," CENTCOM said. President Donald Trump went further: "There may come a point when we are no longer able to be reasonable, and will be forced to militarily complete the job that we very successfully started. If that happens, the Islamic Republic of Iran will no longer exist!"

Iran's response was swift. State broadcaster IRIB reported that the Revolutionary Guards fired back at US-linked military targets. Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy's regional headquarters, reported an Iranian drone attack on its territory. Iran's foreign ministry characterised its actions as "defensive."

The exchange is the worst escalation since Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed the interim peace deal on June 18. That agreement was built around two core provisions: Iran would ensure safe passage for commercial vessels through Hormuz, and the US would sustain a ceasefire that included a halt to hostilities in Lebanon. Neither has fully materialised.



> **"Iran's foreign ministry characterised its actions as "defensive."

The exchange is the worst escalation since Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed the interim peace deal on June 18."**


Iran accuses Washington of not upholding its promise to end fighting in Lebanon. Israeli forces remain in an expanded occupation zone in southern Lebanon, and an Israeli drone struck Nabatieh on Saturday, hours after a new Israel-Lebanon security framework was signed. Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem rejected the framework as "null and void" and a "surrender."

At the root of the Hormuz dispute is a fundamental disagreement over who controls the strait. Washington has been promoting a southern shipping lane along the coast of Oman. Tehran wants vessels to use a northern route through Iranian waters, under Iranian supervision, and ultimately aims to charge transit fees. Ebrahim Azizi, head of Iran's parliamentary national security committee, said Saturday that any violation of Iran's shipping instructions would "be met decisively."

For India, the stakes are existential. The country imports roughly 85 per cent of its crude oil, and the Strait of Hormuz has historically been the highway for its Middle Eastern supply. During the four months of conflict, India pivoted sharply toward Russian crude. June arrivals from Russia are expected to hit a record 2.55 million barrels per day — 53.5 per cent of total imports — up from a pre-war average of 23 per cent.

But that lifeline is under threat too. The US sanctions waiver that legalised India's Russian crude purchases expired on June 17, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said during a visit to Bahrain this week that Washington is "still considering" whether to end the exemptions permanently. President Trump will make the final call based on "prevailing market conditions," Rubio indicated.

Just as India needs to pivot back to Middle Eastern crude, the strait is being attacked again. Saudi Aramco only resumed crude loadings at its Ras Tanura terminal on Friday after a four-month suspension — a milestone that helped push Brent crude below $73, down 10 per cent in a single week. But if the attacks continue, the reopening could stall, supply fears could return, and crude could snap back above $80.

India's refiners, meanwhile, are stuck. They are covered through August with existing cargoes, largely from Russia and spot Middle East purchases. They are not rushing to buy Iranian crude despite a temporary US sanctions waiver, because payment mechanisms remain unresolved and compliance risks are too high. And India still has not passed a single rupee of the oil crash on to consumers — domestic fuel prices are unchanged even as Brent has plummeted from its wartime peak of $126 to $72.

Vice President JD Vance, who led the ceasefire negotiations, summed up the American position on X: "Iran signed a ceasefire agreement. We have honoured it. If they have disagreements about how the MOU is being applied, they can pick up the phone. But violence will be met with violence."

Markets are closed for the weekend. That is not a coincidence. In each of the past three weeks, the most aggressive rhetoric and military action have come on Friday and Saturday, giving both sides room to stake out positions and exchange fire without triggering immediate oil-price volatility. Previously, softer positions followed in time for Monday's open.

Whether that pattern holds this time will determine if the ceasefire survives its second week — and whether India's brief energy reprieve was real or just a weekend away from reversing.

*Sources: Reuters; CNN; USA Today; Hindu BusinessLine; Kpler data*
